City of Newark Planning Commission Agenda May 26, 2026 City of Newark PLANNING COMMISSION MEMO F.1 Finding the 2026 -2031 Capital Improvement Plan to be in conformance with the General Plan (MOTION) Background / Discussion On June 27, 2024, the City Council adopted the 2024-2026 Biennial Budget and Capital Improvement Plan. On October 28, 2025, the City’s Planning Commission found amendments to the 2024-2026 Biennial Budget and Capital Improvement Plan to be in conformance with the General Plan. On November 13, 2025, the City Council adopted amendments to the 2024-2026 Biennial Budget and Capital Improvement Plan to include additional parks, buildings, and infrastructure capital improvement projects. On April 23, 2026, the City Council considered and provided feedback on the preliminary list of projects for consideration to be incorporated into the 2027-2031 CIP. A Capital Improvement Plan is a comprehensive strategic plan that identifies, prioritizes, schedules, and determines funding for necessary project execution. The City of Newark's Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) is now a Five-Year plan that is updated on a rolling basis as part of the Biennial Budget process. Guidance on preparing the CIP comes from the City's General Plan, Specific Plans, Master Planning documents, the City's Strategic Priority Areas, direction from City Council, and community input. A CIP Project is generally defined as necessary work or study associated with the improvement (construction, reconstruction, erection, alteration, renovation, demolition, installation, or significant repair work) involving any publicly owned, leased, or operated facility that involves a major (exceeding $25,000 value) City asset that has a useful life exceeding one year, and that can reasonably be started or substantially completed within the CIP timeframe given time, funding, and resource constraints. This definition combines the goals and policies of the City, the concept of asset capitalization used in the field of finance, and the definition of public projects used in the field of public works. There are five types of CIP Projects. Facility Projects consist of the renovation, replacement, or improvement of the public buildings and facilities that the City owns and operates. Infrastructure Projects consist of significant work within the City's right-of-way, such as streets, sidewalks, curbs, gutter, streetlights, traffic signals and associated equipment. New Equipment consists of new vehicles and other significant technology or hardware. Park Projects consist of the renovation, replacement, or improvement of the public parks that the City owns and maintains. Studies consist of large-scale planning and engineering efforts that directly or indirectly impact capital assets Planning Commission Meeting May 26, 2026 The Capital Budgeting Process (Process) to establish projects and associated budgets within the CIP utilizes a structured, transparent, and strategic approach that aligns with prudent public fiscal policies to ensure successful long-term planning, fiscal responsibility, and public accountability. The Process is iterative, dynamic, and occurs concurrently with the Biennial Budget process. The Process begins with updates and/or review of the City's Mission, Vision, Values, strategic plans, priorities and goals. This effort includes review of the City's General Plan, Specific Plans, Master Planning documents, the City's Strategic Priority Areas, direction from City Council, and community input. Potential new projects are identified with a detailed description of purpose and scope of work, rough cost estimates at the time of construction, a preliminary schedule, and potential funding sources. Existing CIP projects are also reviewed with updated purpose and scope of work, updated cost estimates escalated to estimated time of construction, updated schedule, and updated funding sources. Any existing CIP projects that have been completed or are nearing completion are removed from consideration. Balances, revenues, and expenditures for typical project funding as well as staffing and resources are forecasted, analyzed and reviewed within the CIP timeframe. The Process continues with the Project Ranking and Prioritization Process, whereby all projects are evaluated and scored based on an established weighted criteria to determine those projects that will be incorporated into the Draft CIP. Projects that scored high (corresponding to a higher priority) are reviewed by the City's Executive Team to continue for further evaluation, whereas those projects that scored low are removed from consideration. Additional evaluation considers other factors that may warrant projects to be removed from consideration. New projects may be removed or delayed from consideration if there is an upcoming study or effort that has the potential to substantially alter the project priority; if the new project is redundant or conflicts with another higher priority project; or if there isn't sufficient staffing or resources available to execute the project. The Process continues further with workshops or presentations of the draft list of projects and the Draft CIP to the City Council. This provides an opportunity for the City Council as well as the general public to review and provide feedback. The Draft CIP also requires review by the City's Planning Commission for conformance with the City's General Plan as required by State law. Planning Commission review is a necessary step before the City Council formally adopts the Biennial Budget and CIP. Applicable General Plan Goals include: - Goal LU-4: Enhance Newark’s identity as a city of high-quality development that is distinctive from other cities in the Bay Area. - Goal LU-6: Develop a sustainable, transit-oriented development (TOD) comprised of residential, retail, office, park, and open space uses around the site of the planned Dumbarton Rail station on Newark’s west side. - Goal LU-8: Strengthen Old Town Newark as a vibrant, cohesive mixed-use district that honors Newark’s history while embracing its future. Planning Commission Meeting May 26, 2026 - Goal LU-9: Strengthen NewPark Mall and its environs as a community showcase and quality environment for shopping and other compatible uses. - Goal T-1: Plan, fund, design, construct, operate, and maintain all transportation improvements to provide mobility for all users, appropriate to the function and context of each facility. - Goal T-2: Create a citywide pedestrian and bicycle network that provides safe access to destinations within the city, connects to an integrated regional network, and is accessible to users of all ages, abilities, and means. - Goal T-5: A safe, efficient, and well maintained network of roadways that facilitates vehicle travel in and around the City. - Goal T-6: Ensure that the City is well connected to the regional road, rail, air, and port systems, in support of local economic development and mobility goals. - Goal CS-4: Conserve and manage the City’s tree resources and urban forest. - Goal CS-5: Reduce greenhouse gas emissions in Newark and make reduction of the City’s carbon output a high priority. - Goal PR-2: Expand and improve Newark’s parks and recreational facilities to meet existing and future needs. - Goal PR-3: Manage Newark’s parks in a way that enhances their natural qualities, conveys a positive image of the city and its neighborhoods, and fully meets that community’s recreational needs. - Goal PR-5: Improve Newark’s trail system, with a focus on access to the Newark shoreline, and access between the shoreline and Newark neighborhoods. - Goal EH-1: Reduce the potential for injury, harm, property damage, and loss of life resulting from environmental hazards. - Goal EH-5: Fast, efficient, and coordinated response to natural and man-made emergencies and disaster. - Goal EH-6: Maintain the peach and quiet of Newark neighborhoods and promote and environment where noise does not adversely affect sensitive land uses. - Goal HW-2: A community in which physical fitness is supported and encouraged. - Goal HW-7: Safe and secure neighborhoods and public spaces. - Goal CSF-4: Provide responsive police, fire and emergency medical services that ensure the safety of residents, employers, and visitors. Planning Commission Meeting May 26, 2026 Pursuant to Government Code Section 65401, a finding of CIP conformity with the General Plan by the Planning Commission is required. The Biennial Budget and Capital Improvement Plan is tentatively scheduled for recommended adoption by the City Council in June 2026. The CIP is exempt as a project per Section 15262, feasibility and planning studies, of the California Environmental Quality Act. Action – It is recommended that the Planning Commission, by motion, find the 2026-2031 Capital Improvement Plan to be in conformance with the General Plan. This CIP provides a comprehensive strategy for the planning, prioritization, funding, and execution of needed public improvements. Guided by the City's priorities, community input, fiscal forecasting, and sound planning principals, this CIP serves as a critical tool for the responsible stewardship of public resources. The CIP aligns with the City's priorities to foster a safe and healthy community, further economic vitality and housing for all, boost financial resilience and excellence in service delivery, modernize public facilities and infrastructure, and strengthen the community through education and engagement. Key areas of engagement include maintaining and improving our roadway infrastructure; renovating, replacing, and improving our parks; renovating and constructing new facilities; purchasing new equipment; and executing large-scale studies related to capital assets. The CIP includes over 100 projects representing a total planned investment of over $200 million over the five-year CIP planning horizon. The CIP includes notable projects, such as the replacement of City fire stations, a new Cultural Arts Center, and several playground replacement, restroom replacement, and field improvements to various City parks. In addition, the CIP includes necessary equipment, planning studies, and continued prioritization of annual street surfacing, sidewalk, and other roadway and rail crossing safety projects. The City continues to effectively seek, obtain, and utilize a variety of funding sources. The CIP identifies and includes federal, state, regional, and local funding sources, such as grants, fees, and tax revenue. The City's past success in obtaining and effectively utilizing these diverse sources is planned to continue in future years. The CIP is a culmination of an extensive team effort by every department within the City. We would like to acknowledge and thank the tremendous effort by City staff to compile this CIP over a period of several months. Estimates are based on a combination of analyzing recent and similar bid pricing, third-party expert consultant reviews, and engineering judgment. Estimates typically include contingencies consistent with the estimated amount, projected risks, and sound engineering practices. Estimates typically are escalated to represent the anticipated cost at the projected time of bidding. Capital Improvement Project Ranking and Prioritization Process Project prioritization is based on standards established by the Government Finance Officers Association. Projects are prioritized and scored based on evaluating eight weighted criteria below. The maximum possible score is 125 points, and those projects with the higher scores have a higher priority. Project scores from 95 to 125 are "Critical Priority"; 70 to 94 are "High Priority"; 45-69 are "Medium Priority"; and below 45 are "Low Priority."

Overview Department Project Type STUDIES Project Number CIP001401 Description A feasibility study assessing rental housing stock in the City of Newark and determining the need for a Rental Inspection program. This study will also prescribe funding sources and implementation of the program, which is expected to be a costrecovery model funded by licensing or permitting costs paid by property owners who are part of the program, assess if current staffing levels will support such a program, and determine the cadence of proactive inspections. The cadence of the inspections may be determined by items such as the age of the building, number of units, permit history, and a history of complaints. Owners of rental properties are responsible for maintaining their buildings in compliance with minimum housing standards. Newark currently depends on complaints from tenants to investigate allegations of substandard housing. Often, these investigations result in finding violations that impact not only the initial tenant but also the health and safety of all the occupants. Tenants are often hesitant to report substandard housing conditions for fear of retaliation, up to and including eviction. A proactive inspection program would allow Newark to inspect rental stock to ensure they meet minimum housing standards and that all building maintenance and repairs are done in accordance with current building codes. A proactive inspection program ensures our residents are afforded a clean, safe, and healthy place to live.
